welcome.title: Help shape the next year of PyPSA
intro: PyPSA is developed by a small team and a wide community. We want to spend our development time on what helps you most. With this survey we want to learn how you use PyPSA, which features you would like to see and where we can make your experience with PyPSA more productive.

bullets.text: How long the survey takes: 10 to 15 minutes. You can skip any question and any feature section that is not relevant to you.

What do we use the results for? We publish the results on pypsa.org and use them to set the development priorities for the next year. We repeat the survey every six months, so you can see what changed.
We do not ask for your name. Organisation and links are optional and never published with your answers. We publish results only in aggregate.
Your answers are stored in the EU. Details are on our

welcome.support: Resources for conducting this survey and for implementing its findings are supported by Breakthrough Energy GRIDS.

part3.title: Part 3: Rate the roadmap
part3.intro: The PyPSA maintainers have collected candidate features for the next year across different areas. They come from the public roadmap, from feature requests on GitHub and from a comparison with commercial planning tools. They are candidates, not promises. Your ratings decide which ones we build first.
part3.howItWorks: How it works. For each feature, tell us how important it is for your work in the next year. Each feature has a one-sentence explanation under its name. Skip anything you have no view on, a blank counts as no answer.
part3.scaleQuestion: How important is this for your work in the next year?

nonUser.q2_1Title: What would you use PyPSA for?

thankYou.text: Thank you for your time. We will publish the results on pypsa.org soon and announce them on the mailing list, Discord and GitHub. The ratings feed directly into the next round of prioritisation.

pages.name: p3_1
pages.title: Investment and pathway planning
pages.description: Deciding what to build, retire and keep, and when.

elements.name: q3_1
elements.title: How important is this for your work in the next year?

rows.text: Let the model retire or retrofit assets early
rows.description: Economic phase-out and repowering decisions instead of fixed technical lifetimes.

rows.text: Technology costs that fall with deployment (endogenous learning)
rows.description: Learning curves inside the model, so early investment lowers later costs.

rows.text: Fixed cost per unit built
rows.description: A cost per installed unit, independent of its size, for discrete assets like transformers.

rows.text: Trade off several objectives (multi-objective optimisation)
rows.description: Explore the best trade-offs between cost, emissions, land use or import dependence.

rows.text: Limit how fast capacity can be built depending on what's built in earlier years
rows.description: Build-rate caps that depend on what was built in earlier years.

rows.text: Investments that adapt as uncertainty resolves
rows.description: Decide now, adjust later as costs or policies become known, for example a hydrogen pipeline built only if the carbon price rises.

rows.text: See which inputs drive your results (global sensitivity analysis)
rows.description: Sample uncertain inputs, run many networks with Monte Carlo and rank the inputs by their effect on the results.

elements.name: q3_1_other
elements.title: Anything missing in this area?

pages.name: p3_2
pages.title: Operations, reliability and markets
pages.description: Running the system and keeping supply secure.

elements.name: q3_2
elements.title: How important is this for your work in the next year?

rows.text: Richer unit commitment
rows.description: More operational constraints, for example start-up trajectories or ramping costs.

rows.text: Operating reserves and capacity margins
rows.description: Reserve requirements to which eligible assets contribute spare capacity.

rows.text: Cost of changing dispatch (ramping costs)
rows.description: Penalise ramping between hours, for example for wear or balancing exposure.

rows.text: Allow constraints to be violated at a price
rows.description: Penalties instead of an infeasible model.

rows.text: Loss-of-load and unserved-energy metrics
rows.description: Probabilistic adequacy indicators from outage-sampled runs, including capacity credit.

rows.text: Strategic bidding of market players (Cournot)
rows.description: Markup or oligopoly behaviour instead of perfect competition.

rows.text: Orchestration layer for connecting multiple PyPSA model instances
rows.description: For instance, pass capacities from a planning run to a weekly hydro or maintenance schedule and on to hourly dispatch with market stages. Or run day-ahead market followed by redispatch and congestion management.

elements.name: q3_2_other
elements.title: Anything missing in this area?

pages.name: p3_3
pages.title: Grid physics and sector networks
pages.description: More realistic networks for electricity, gas, heat and water.

elements.name: q3_3
elements.title: How important is this for your work in the next year?

rows.text: Voltage and losses in distribution grids (DistFlow)
rows.description: Linearised power flow for radial networks with PV, batteries, heat pumps and EV charging.

rows.text: Devices that steer power flows (SSSC, UPFC)
rows.description: Series compensators and flow controllers as optimisable components.

rows.text: Reactive power and voltage limits in optimisation
rows.description: Convex relaxation of AC power flow in addition to today's DC approximation.

rows.text: Hand results to power flow tools (pandapower, PowSyBl)
rows.description: Export optimised networks for AC, short-circuit and dynamic checks.

rows.text: Pressure-driven gas pipeline flow (Weymouth)
rows.description: Linearised pipeline physics with nodal pressures and linepack storage.

rows.text: Temperature levels in heat networks
rows.description: District heating with supply and return temperatures as model states.

rows.text: Hydro cascades with water travel times and reservoir head
rows.description: Linked reservoirs with delays, spillage and fill-level dependent efficiency.

elements.title: Anything missing in this area?

elements.name: q3_4
elements.title: How important is this for your work in the next year?

rows.text: Explore a solved network in a dashboard
rows.description: Launch a local app with statistics, plots and maps.

rows.text: Market statistics out of the box
rows.description: Price duration curves, congestion rents, market values and asset revenues.

rows.text: Financial metrics per asset
rows.description: Net present value, levelised cost and payback.

rows.text: Map results back to the original grid (disaggregation)
rows.description: Disaggregate clustered results to the original nodes and assets.

rows.text: Compare scenarios side by side
rows.description: Load several runs and difference them in statistics and plots.

elements.name: q3_4_other
elements.title: Anything missing in this area?

pages.name: p3_5
pages.title: Data, input and output
pages.description: Getting models in and out of PyPSA.

elements.name: q3_5
elements.title: How important is this for your work in the next year?

rows.text: Read and write model equations as text
rows.description: Declare custom constraints without code and export the full formulation as readable maths for papers and audits.

rows.text: Open large networks faster
rows.description: Load lazily only the parts of a network you need, also from cloud storage, instead of the whole file.

rows.text: Import grid models from industry formats
rows.description: Read these files directly from CIM-CGMES, MATPOWER, or PSS/E.

rows.text: Store and exchange models in a tool-neutral format
rows.description: A declared schema that other frameworks and databases can read, with scenario variants that store only their differences, and nothing lost on save and reload.

rows.text: Catch input errors before solving (validation)
rows.description: Stricter checks with clear messages on what is inconsistent and where.

rows.text: Units on buses and attributes
rows.description: Declare units once and have them checked and carried through to results.

rows.text: Define your own component types and properties
rows.description: Add components and shared properties, such as carriers, next to the built-in ones.

rows.text: Directly access data from adjacent tools
rows.description: More heavy data integration of cost assumptions from technology-data, renewable time series from atlite, power plants from powerplantmatching.

pages.description: Where your models hit their limits.

elements.name: q3_6_1
elements.title: Have you hit computational limits with PyPSA in the last year?

choices.text: Building the model took too long
The solver struggled numerically, for example slow convergence or spurious infeasibility

elements.name: q3_6_2
elements.title: What did you do about it?

choices.text: Reduced spatial resolution, for example by clustering
Reduced temporal resolution or used representative periods
Split the horizon, for example rolling horizon
Used a bigger machine or a cluster

elements.name: q3_6_3
elements.title: How much larger would you like your models to be than what you run today, for example in buses, snapshots or scenarios?

elements.name: q3_6
elements.title: How important is this for your work in the next year?

rows.text: Solve models too large for one solve (decomposition)
rows.description: Split into coordinated subproblems, for example Benders for investment and dispatch or SDDP for long storage horizons.

rows.text: Mix time resolutions in one model
rows.description: Hourly where it matters, coarser elsewhere, per bus or carrier.

rows.text: Reduce many scenarios to a few
rows.description: Generate and reduce scenario sets from weather years, outages or price paths.

rows.text: Run many scenarios in parallel
rows.description: Launch and collect a batch of runs locally or on a cluster from one call.

elements.name: q4_1
elements.title: What slows you down when you work with PyPSA, and what is missing?
elements.description: Anything counts: installation, learning, documentation, error messages, debugging infeasible models, build or solve time, memory, changes between versions, custom constraints, data preparation, analysis, lack of graphical user interface, finding help, or a feature that was not on the list. Be concrete about what you were trying to do.
